name: Glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas Pathway)
description: Glycolysis in E. coli is the central pathway for glucose catabolism, converting one glucose molecule to two pyruvate molecules while producing 2 ATP (net) and 2 NADH. The pathway consists of 10 enzyme-catalyzed steps divided into two phases: the energy investment phase (steps 1-5, consuming 2 ATP) and the energy payoff phase (steps 6-10, producing 4 ATP and 2 NADH). E. coli has metabolic flexibility with alternative enzymes at several steps: glucose can enter via phosphotransferase system (PTS) or permease, different phosphofructokinases exist (Pfk-1 and Pfk-2), and pyruvate has multiple fates (TCA cycle, fermentation, or biosynthesis). The pathway is regulated by allosteric effectors (PEP inhibits Pfk, AMP activates), phosphorylation, and transcriptional control. This flowchart illustrates the complete pathway, alternative routes, regulatory mechanisms, and metabolic branch points.
scientificAccuracy: This flowchart is based on comprehensive biochemical characterization of E. coli glycolytic enzymes. All enzymes, intermediates, cofactors, regulatory mechanisms, and alternative pathways have been extensively validated. The model represents the canonical glycolytic pathway with bacterial-specific features.

notes: Glycolysis is the most ancient and conserved metabolic pathway, present in nearly all organisms. E. coli's version has bacterial-specific features including PTS for glucose uptake and Pfk-2 as an alternative phosphofructokinase. The pathway demonstrates metabolic flexibility with pyruvate having multiple fates (oxidation, fermentation, biosynthesis) depending on oxygen availability. Phosphofructokinase (Pfk) is the committed and rate-limiting step, subject to allosteric regulation by energy charge. Under anaerobiosis, E. coli performs mixed-acid fermentation producing lactate, ethanol, formate, and acetate to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis. The pathway is essential for both catabolism and anabolism, providing precursors for biosynthesis.
